questions.q: What makes a pair of states a valid measurement basis for a qubit?
options: Only {|0⟩,|1⟩} can ever be used — all other pairs are notational tricks, not real measurement bases
Any pair of states that is orthonormal — each normalized and mutually orthogonal to the other
Any two states that have the same amplitude magnitudes
Any two states produced by applying the Hadamard gate
questions.explain: A valid measurement basis just needs to be orthonormal: both states normalized and orthogonal to each other. The computational basis is one example; {|+⟩,|−⟩} (the X-basis) is another equally valid one.

questions.q: What is the result of measuring |0⟩ in the X-basis {|+⟩,|−⟩}?
options: P(+) = 1, P(−) = 0, since |0⟩ is a definite state
P(+) = 0.5, P(−) = 0.5, an even split
The X-basis cannot be used to measure |0⟩ at all
questions.explain: The overlaps |⟨+|0⟩|² and |⟨−|0⟩|² are both 0.5, so measuring |0⟩ in the X-basis gives an exact 50/50 split between + and − outcomes, even though |0⟩ is 'definite' in the computational basis.

questions.q: |0⟩ is a definite, non-superposed state in the computational basis, yet gives a 50/50 split when measured in the X-basis. What does this show?
options: That |0⟩ is secretly unstable and randomly changes between measurements
That whether a state looks 'definite' or 'superposed' depends on the chosen measurement basis, not on some absolute property of the state alone
That the X-basis measurement is simply wrong and should be disregarded
That |0⟩ and |+⟩ are actually the same state written two different ways
questions.explain: The qubit's state |0⟩ never changes — what changes is which basis you compare it against. 'Definite' and 'superposed' are properties relative to a chosen basis, not intrinsic, basis-free labels on the state.

questions.q: Why is basis-dependence described as physically real rather than a notational trick?
options: Because running the X-basis measurement on |0⟩ produces genuinely random, experimentally verifiable + / − outcomes 50/50 of the time — not a relabeled but secretly deterministic result
Because it isn't physically real — it's purely a mathematical convenience with no experimental consequence
Because the X-basis only works in theory, never on real hardware
Because measuring in different bases always gives the exact same statistics regardless of the state
questions.explain: The randomness from measuring |0⟩ in the X-basis is a real, repeatable, experimentally verifiable physical outcome — genuine 50/50 randomness, not a relabeling of an underlying deterministic fact.

questions.q: Why does choice of measurement basis matter for quantum algorithm and protocol design, rather than being an afterthought?
options: It doesn't matter — any basis gives identical information about a state

Because which basis you measure in determines what information gets extracted, and the same deliberate basis-choice idea is what entanglement/Bell-inequality tests in chapter 4 rely on to reveal correlations
Because only the computational basis is ever used in real quantum hardware
Because basis choice only affects classical post-processing, never the quantum circuit itself
questions.explain: Measuring in the wrong basis can hide the very information an algorithm or protocol is trying to extract. Chapter 4's Bell-inequality tests are a direct application: they depend on deliberately comparing measurement statistics across different chosen bases.
